Ford Drops New 2028 Mustang GTD 1901, It’s a Special Edition That Honors the Past
11 photos
Photo: Ford
It’s been more than three years since Ford pulled the wraps off the Mustang GTD , a street-version of its GT3 racer that was introduced for the 2025 model year, with a suffix that stands for Grand Touring Daytona, and the company now has a new special edition version of this model.
Nope, it’s not the GTD Competition, which managed to lap the Nurburgring in an impressive 6:40.835 earlier this year, boasting revised aerodynamics, fresh rubber, some weight-saving measures and more oomph over the regular GTD, but something that looks at the past. It’s called the GTD 1901, and it is an homage to Henry Ford’s first racer.
The Blue Oval hadn’t yet been founded when Henry Ford built the 26-horsepower, 8.8-liter, two-cylinder race car called the Sweepstakes. He put it through its paces on a dirt track outside Detroit, and since he was pretty much a raw novice, the odds were against him. However, in the end, he won the race, and took home a $1,000 cash prize, which is roughly $40,000 today, as well as a glass punch bowl, and made a name for himself.
A Scientific American article noted that the racer “ possesses features entitling it to credit as being the most unconventional, if not the most beautiful, design so far produced by American ingenuity. ” The recognition and credibility from that historic race allowed Henry Ford to secure the financing needed to start his second company (after the Detroit Automobile Company in 1900), and that is Ford Motor Company, which still exists today.
Photo: Ford Ford’s new Mustang GTD 1901 is a 2028 model year car, and pretty much a livery package that follows in the footsteps of the GTD Spirit of America. It replaces the latter, and just like it, it benefits from the Performance Package, which is standard. This includes underbody flaps, a unique face with dive planes, an active rear wing, a bigger splitter attached to the front bumper, and less sound deadening.
The chin spoiler, rocker, diffuser, and wing have exposed carbon fiber accents on them, and besides these, the new model also debuts the magnesium wheels, which are available, and reduce the car’s weight by 50.3 pounds (22.8 kg), according to the automaker. A new painted racing stripe option has also been added to the Mustang GTD, thus enhancing the customization choices available for this model.
By the way, the available magnesium wheels were supposed to be offered on the regular GTD when it launched for the 2025 model year, but they ended up being delayed. These wheels will also be available on the non-1901 versions of the GTD in black or luster nickel, and the Blue Oval is considering launching them as a retrofit option for current GTD owners who want to upgrade their rides.
Painted stripes instead of decals are another novelty, and the rare and eye-wateringly expensive muscle car also benefits from full-grain leather trim on the center console, dashboard panel, and door cards when it comes to the new Ford Mustang GTD 1901. The gear selector dial and the titanium paddle shifters, with the latter being part of the optional titanium trim package, have also been redesigned.
Beneath the skin lies the same Multimatic suspension with inboard springs and dampers at the rear, which can be watched through a dedicated window inside, and the model also benefits from the familiar supercharged V8, making 815 horsepower, and an eight-speed dual-clutch transmission.
Photo: Ford Details surrounding the pricing and availability of the new Ford Mustang GTD 1901 haven’t yet been disclosed, though the company noted that around 20 percent of the total production will comprise the 1901 model. Deliveries are scheduled to commence in the second quarter of 2027, and the Benjamins haven’t been mentioned. Nevertheless, interested parties should expect to pay over $400,000 for such a thing, which is pretty much new-gen supercar money.
Would you add a 1901 version of the Ford Mustang GTD to your collection if money were the least of your concerns? What about a regular GTD? Or would you perhaps wait for the brand to drop the new Mustang GTD Competition, with its unspecified power increase, and other changes?
You should know that for roughly $400K, your could buy a new supercar, like the Lamborghini Temerario, which has 907 horsepower (920 ps/677 kW) available via the right pedal. That’s how much the plug-in hybrid 4-liter twin-turbo V8 develops in total, enabling a 213 mph (343 kph) top speed, and 0-62 mph (0-97 kph) in 2.7 seconds.
There is also a Ford Mustang Dark Horse SC on sale, which kicks off at $106,090 (MSRP), and features a supercharged 5.2-liter V8 engine rated at 795 hp (806 ps/593 kW). But is the Mustang GTD (1901) roughly four times the car? You be the judge of that, and don’t forget to drop a few lines below to reveal your impression on this new 2028 MY muscle car.
